text: God commands all people everywhere to repent. Whoever turns from sin and trusts in Christ alone is forgiven and has eternal life: by grace, through faith, not by works. Following Him costs everything, and no one who comes to Him is turned away. (Mark 1:15; Acts 17:30; John 3:16; Eph 2:8–9; Rom 10:9–13; Luke 14:27–28; John 6:37) "What is keeping you from turning to Christ today?"

label: The Gospel
title: The short version: the Romans Road
text: When you only have a minute, walk these in order, and call them to repent. (Rom 3:23; Rom 6:23; Rom 5:8; Acts 17:30; Rom 10:9–10; Rom 10:13; Rom 8:1)

label: The Gospel
title: How to walk someone through it
text: For a step-by-step way to do this in a real conversation, using the Ten Commandments first and then the cross, open The Way of the Master.

label: The Gospel
title: If they respond
text: Pray with them. Get them a Bible and get them into a church that preaches it, where they can be baptized by immersion as a believer. Follow up. Don't pronounce them saved. Point them to Christ, and let assurance grow from following Him. (Acts 2:41–42; Matt 28:19–20; 2 Cor 13:5; 1 John 2:3–6; John 8:31)

label: The Gospel
title: If they don't
text: Stay warm and leave the door open. You plant and water; God gives the growth. (1 Cor 3:6–7; 1 Pet 3:15–16; 2 Tim 2:24–26)

label: For any conversation
title: The Way of the Master
text: Use the law to reach the conscience, then give the gospel. God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble (James 4:6), so: law to the proud, grace to the humble. The Ten Commandments work like a mirror: they show a person their sin so that the cross makes sense. Jesus did this with the rich young ruler. (Rom 3:19–20; Rom 7:7; Gal 3:24; Mark 10:17–22)

label: The Way of the Master
title: 1. Start with an everyday question
text: Move from ordinary talk to spiritual things with one question. "What do you think happens after we die?"

label: The Way of the Master
title: 2. Are you a good person?
text: Almost everyone says yes. Let them say it. (Prov 20:6) "Would you consider yourself a good person?"

label: The Way of the Master
title: 3. Have you kept the Ten Commandments?
text: Walk through a few, one at a time, and let them answer each. (Ex 20:1–17) "Have you ever told a lie? What does that make you?" "Have you ever taken anything that wasn't yours, whatever its value?" "Have you ever used God's name as a curse word?" Jesus said that looking with lust is adultery in the heart. "Have you ever done that?" (Matt 5:27–28) Jesus put anger under the command "You shall not murder" (Matt 5:21–22), and John says whoever hates his brother is a murderer (1 John 3:15).

label: The Way of the Master
title: 4. Judgment: innocent or guilty?
text: Sum up what they admitted in their own words, then ask. (Heb 9:27; Rom 2:15–16; James 2:10) "If God judges you by that standard, will you be innocent or guilty?"

label: The Way of the Master
title: 5. Destiny: heaven or hell?
text: Don't soften it, and don't gloat. Say it because you care where they end up. (Rev 21:8; 1 Cor 6:9–10) "Would that be heaven or hell? Does that concern you?"

label: The Way of the Master
title: 6. Now give the good news
text: You stand guilty in God's courtroom, and Someone steps in and pays your fine in full. That is what Christ did on the cross, and He rose from the dead. (Rom 5:8; 2 Cor 5:21; 1 Pet 2:24; 1 Cor 15:3–4)

label: The Way of the Master
title: 7. Repent and trust
text: Believing a parachute exists won't save you; you have to put it on. Turn from sin and put your trust in Christ alone, today. (Acts 3:19; Acts 20:21; Rom 13:14; 2 Cor 6:2) "When are you going to do that?"

label: The Way of the Master
title: Keep in mind
text: Already humble? If someone is broken over their sin, skip the law and go straight to grace. answering objections clears the path, but the law and the gospel do the work. Don't spend an hour on arguments and never get here. (Rom 2:15) kind, patient, and plainly concerned for them. (2 Tim 2:24–26) Then go back to The Gospel for the full message and what to do when they respond.

label: For any conversation
title: Worldviews: how do you know?
text: Everyone starts somewhere. Only God's word gives you ground to stand on. A presupposition is what a person takes for granted before the argument starts. The atheist is not neutral, and neither are you. He already knows God and suppresses that truth (Rom 1:18–21), so you are not handing him a God he has never met. You are showing him that he leans on God every time he reasons, judges or trusts his own mind. (Prov 1:7; Col 2:3; Ps 14:1; 1 Cor 1:20)

label: Worldviews: how do you know?
title: What you are showing
text: You are not saying he knows nothing or believes in nothing. He reasons, does science and knows right from wrong, because he lives in God's world and is made in God's image. You are saying his worldview cannot account for any of it, and yours can. He is using the tools God gave him to argue against God. "We both use reason. I'm not asking whether you reason. I'm asking why reason can be trusted if your view is true."

label: Worldviews: how do you know?
title: Step 1: Don't give up your ground
text: Do not agree to set the Bible aside and argue from "neutral" facts. No one is neutral, and Scripture is the standard, not the thing on trial. You start from what God has revealed. He starts from his own guess. (Prov 26:4; 2 Cor 10:5; 1 Pet 3:15) "Would you set aside your trust in reason to prove reason? Then why should I set aside God's word?"

label: Worldviews: how do you know?
title: Step 2: Ask what he would accept
text: Before you give evidence, find out what he counts as evidence. If he has no standard, he has no basis for saying there isn't any. "What would count as evidence for you?" "Only what can be measured or tested." → "Did you measure that? Which experiment showed that only tested things are true?" That rule is not something the five senses can find. "I don't know what would convince me." → "Then how do you know there's no evidence?" "God is outside the universe, so He can't be tested." → Evidence is more than lab results. We reason, weigh testimony and draw conclusions every day. (Acts 1:3; Heb 11:1)

label: Worldviews: how do you know?
title: Step 3: Step into his view and show it cannot stand
text: Take his view on its own terms and ask what follows. One question at a time, and wait for the answer. (Prov 26:5) "How do you know that? How do you know anything for certain?" If he says we can't know anything for certain: "Are you certain of that?" "Are the laws of logic made of matter? Do they change? Where do unchanging, universal laws come from in a universe of matter in motion?" If he says God is illogical: "That assumes logic is reliable. In your view, where does it come from?" "You said 'mind.' Is that anything more than brain chemistry? If your thoughts are chemistry shaped for survival, why trust them to tell you what is true?" "Why expect nature to act tomorrow the way it did today?" (Gen 8:22; Col 1:17; Heb 1:3) "If we came from nothing and go to nothing, on what basis does anything you do matter?" If he says nothing has meaning: "Does that sentence have meaning?" (Eccl 1:2; Eccl 12:13–14)

label: Worldviews: how do you know?
title: Right and wrong
text: Start here when he calls something evil, unfair or hateful. "Is morality objective, or is it opinion?" "It's subjective." → "Then you can't say I'm wrong. You can only say you prefer something else, the way one person prefers burgers and another pizza." Watch for him to keep saying you are wrong anyway. Point it out kindly. "It comes from my experience." → "Someone raised to hate his neighbors has experience too. Is his hatred good?" Experience differs from person to person, so it cannot be the standard. "It comes from science." → Science tells you what is. It cannot tell you what ought to be. "Which experiment shows that lying is wrong?" "That's just your interpretation of the Bible." → Everyone interprets something: he interprets data and his own experience. Disagreement does not cancel truth. "If someone says 1 + 1 = 3, does that make the answer uncertain?" "That's true for you. This is my truth." → An opinion is not the same as truth. Truth is what matches reality, whoever believes it. "Can a person sincerely believe something and be wrong?" "It's objective." → "Then who set the standard, and why does it bind everyone?" (Rom 2:14–15)

label: Worldviews: how do you know?
title: Start with the Creator
text: Many people today have no Bible background. Words like sin, judgment and Savior mean little to someone who thinks he is an accident. Peter preached to people who knew the Scriptures and went straight to Christ and repentance (Acts 2:22–38). Paul, in Athens, began with the God who made the world and everything in it, and then said God now commands all people everywhere to repent (Acts 17:24–31). John's Gospel begins the same way: all things came into being through Christ (John 1:1–3; Col 1:16). You are not delaying the gospel. You are telling him whose world this is, so that sin makes sense and the cross is good news. "Who made you? And if you were made, who do you answer to?" Made on purpose. He is not a cosmic accident. He was made by God, in God's image, to know Him. (Gen 1:27; Ps 100:3; Ps 139:13–14) Worth. Every person bears God's image: unborn, disabled, old, unable to contribute anything. "If worth depends on what a person can do, is a strong man worth more than a child with Down syndrome?" (Gen 9:6; James 3:9) Guilt. He may have been taught that guilt is only herd instinct or upbringing. "When someone wrongs you, is that only instinct, or did he really do wrong?" The conscience is God's law written on the heart. (Rom 2:14–15) Then sin and the Savior. The One who made him is the One he has sinned against, and the One who came to die for sinners. (Col 1:16; Col 1:19–20)

label: Worldviews: how do you know?
title: Step 4: Bring him back to your ground
text: Show that what he has been borrowing belongs to God. Logic reflects God's unchanging mind, morality His holy character, the order of nature His faithfulness, and our reasoning His image in us. All things were made through the Word. (Gen 1:27; Mal 3:6; John 1:1–3; Acts 17:24–28)

label: Worldviews: how do you know?
title: If he says
text: "So you're saying atheists can't know anything?" → No. He knows a great deal. The question is whether his worldview can explain how. "I just lack belief. I don't have to prove anything." → "You still reason, judge and trust your mind every day. What do those rest on?" "That's circular. You're using God to prove God." → Every final starting point has to vouch for itself, or it isn't final. "Can you prove your words have meaning without using words?" The question is which starting point makes sense of everything else. His explains nothing. God's word explains logic, morality, science and him. (Heb 6:13) "We both just assume our senses work." → For him the senses are the foundation, with nothing under them. For you they are a tool, and under them is the God who made eyes, minds and the world they fit. "Logic is just a fact of the universe." → That repeats the claim; it doesn't explain it. "Would you accept it if I said God is just a fact of the universe?" "Logic is just how humans think." → Then it could have been otherwise, and it would not bind anyone who thinks differently, including you. "Morality comes from evolution or society." → That tells you what people do approve of, not what they ought to. Was slavery right when society approved it? "I don't know where they come from, and that's fine." → "So you rely on them with no reason to. That is faith. I can tell you where they come from."

label: Worldviews: how do you know?
title: Watch out
text: Don't say "you believe in nothing." He will name things he believes, and he'll be right. Say his worldview can't account for them. Don't call him or his view dumb, and don't dismiss him. Say "that doesn't hold together," and stay kind when he gets sharp. (2 Tim 2:24–26) Don't blame evil on God's hands being tied. When evil or hell comes up, don't say God wanted to stop it but free will prevented Him. God is sovereign over all things, He is not the author of sin, and people answer for their own sin. Use the evil and suffering answer and the "why create me?" answer. (Eph 1:11; Gen 50:20; Acts 2:23) Don't trade away creation to sound reasonable. God made everything in six days. See the evolution answer. The full case is on The fallacy of evolution. Don't treat it as a trick. Winning the exchange saves no one. He is not confused; he is suppressing the truth, and only God opens blind eyes. (2 Cor 4:4–6; 1 Cor 2:14) Evidence still belongs. The apostles pointed to the empty tomb and the eyewitnesses. Give the evidence as God's facts, not as something a neutral judge gets to rule on. (Acts 17:31; 1 Cor 15:3–8) Don't lean on quotes and numbers you can't back up. A line credited to Darwin or a statistic from a sermon can be wrong, and one bad quote costs you the hearing. Stay with Scripture and with questions. Get to the cross. This clears the ground. Then give The Gospel. For a short version to run live, open the borrowed capital play.

label: For any conversation
title: The problem of evil
text: Why does a good God allow suffering? This is the question behind most unbelief, and often it is not an argument but a wound. Find out which before you answer. Scripture does not explain every sorrow. It tells us who rules over suffering, where it came from, what God has done about it, and how it ends. (Deut 29:29; Rom 8:28)

label: The problem of evil
title: First, listen
text: "Is this a question you're thinking through, or something you're living through?" If he is hurting, sit with him before you reason with him. Job's friends did well for seven days, until they opened their mouths. Weep with those who weep. (Job 2:13; Rom 12:15; John 11:35)

label: The problem of evil
title: What you are showing
text: To call anything evil, he needs a real standard of good that stands above every person and culture. In a universe of matter and chance there is suffering, but there is no "ought not." The complaint itself borrows from the God it is aimed at. See Morality and justice. "When you say that's evil, do you mean you dislike it, or that it is really wrong? By what standard?"

label: The problem of evil
title: What Scripture says
text: God made the world very good. Evil is not part of what He made. (Gen 1:31) Sin brought death and suffering in. Man rebelled, and the whole creation was subjected to futility. (Gen 3:17–19; Rom 5:12; Rom 8:20–22) God is sovereign over all of it, and He is not the author of sin. Nothing happens outside His rule, and He tempts no one. (Eph 1:11; Isa 45:7; James 1:13; 1 John 1:5) He means for good what men mean for evil. Joseph's brothers sold him; God sent him to save lives. (Gen 50:20; Rom 8:28) The cross is the clearest case. The worst evil ever done, the murder of the Son of God, was carried out by lawless men and was God's predetermined plan to save sinners. If God can bring the greatest good out of the greatest evil, He can be trusted with the rest. (Acts 2:23; Acts 4:27–28) He does not owe us an account. When Job asked why, God answered with Himself. (Job 38:1–4; Job 42:1–6; Rom 9:20) He entered it. Our God is not far off from pain. He became a man of sorrows. (Isa 53:3–5; Heb 4:15) He will end it. Every wrong will be judged, and every tear wiped away. (Rev 21:3–4; Acts 17:31; Rom 8:18)

label: The problem of evil
title: If they say
text: "A good God would stop evil." → He will, and on a set day. The harder question is what happens to us when He does, since the evil is not only out there. He waits because He is patient. (2 Pet 3:9; Rom 2:4) "If God removed all evil at midnight tonight, where would that leave you and me?" "Why doesn't He stop it now?" → We are not told every reason, and a God big enough to blame is big enough to have reasons we cannot see. What we are told is that He is working all things together for good for those who love Him. (Rom 8:28; Isa 55:8–9) "What about natural disasters and disease?" → They belong to a creation that groans under the curse, and Jesus says they are a call to repent, not proof that the victims were worse than we are. (Rom 8:20–22; Luke 13:1–5) "What about children who suffer?" → Do not hurry this one. God is the defender of the helpless and will judge every hand raised against a child. Our own outrage is His image in us. (Ps 10:14; Matt 18:6; Gen 18:25) "I prayed and He didn't answer." → Paul prayed three times, and Christ prayed in Gethsemane. The answer was grace to bear it, and then resurrection. (2 Cor 12:8–9; Matt 26:39) "Then God is the cause of evil." → No. Men do evil from their own hearts and are fully responsible for it. God rules over it for holy ends without doing it. Scripture holds both together in one sentence. (Acts 2:23; James 1:13–14)

label: The problem of evil
title: Watch out
text: Don't say God's hands were tied by our free will. He is never helpless. Say He is sovereign and good, and that He has purposes. Don't explain a particular tragedy. You do not know why this child died or that cancer came. Say so. (Deut 29:29) Don't answer a wound with an argument. Know which one is in front of you. Don't leave out the cross. It is the only place the problem of evil is answered and not only discussed.

label: The problem of evil
title: Bring it to the gospel
text: The real question is not why bad things happen to good people. There was only one good Person, and He volunteered. He suffered for sinners so that suffering would not have the last word over them. (1 Pet 3:18; 2 Cor 5:21; Rom 8:32) "God did something about evil at the cross. Have you ever looked at what He did there for you?" Then give The Gospel.

label: For any conversation
title: Morality and justice
text: Can morality exist without God? Everyone you meet believes some things are really wrong. Your aim is to show that only the God of Scripture makes sense of that, and that the same God who gives the law will judge by it. (Rom 2:14–16; Acts 17:31)

label: Morality and justice
title: What you are showing
text: You are not saying an unbeliever cannot be kind, honest or brave. He can, because he is made in God's image and God's law is written on his heart. You are saying he cannot account for right and wrong. He can know it, and he cannot explain why it binds anyone. (Rom 2:14–15; Gen 1:27) "Is anything wrong for everyone, everywhere, whether they agree or not? What makes it so?"

label: Morality and justice
title: Where the standard comes from
text: Good is what God is. He does not look up to a standard above Him, and He does not invent it on a whim. Righteousness and justice are the foundation of His throne. (Ps 89:14; Deut 32:4; 1 John 1:5) He has told us. What is good is not a mystery. (Mic 6:8; Ex 20:1–17; Matt 22:37–40) It is written on every heart. That is why cultures everywhere punish murder, theft and betrayal. (Rom 2:14–15) People matter because God made them. Human worth does not come from usefulness or strength. (Gen 9:6; James 3:9)

label: Morality and justice
title: Why the other answers fail
text: "Each person decides." → Then no one is ever wrong, including the man who robs him. He will not live by that. "Society decides." → Then the reformer is always the villain. Slavery was legal, and the people who opposed it were breaking society's rules. "Was slavery right when most people approved of it?" "Evolution gave us morals." → That would explain why we feel them, not why we must obey them. Survival also rewards cruelty and deceit. "Whatever reduces suffering." → Why should anyone care about a stranger's suffering? That is already a moral rule, and it needs a source. "Science tells us." → Science describes what is. It cannot tell you what ought to be. "Is it good because God commands it, or does He command it because it's good?" → Neither. It is good because it reflects who He is, and His nature does not change. (Mal 3:6; James 1:17)

label: Morality and justice
title: Justice needs a Judge
text: Most wrongs are never put right in this life. Killers die in their beds. If death ends everything, justice is a wish. (Eccl 8:14; Ps 73:3–17) God will bring every act into judgment. That is good news for every victim. (Eccl 12:14; Rom 2:5–6; Rev 20:11–13) It is hard news for all of us. The standard we use on others will be used on us, and none of us has kept even our own. (Rom 2:1; Rom 3:19; Rom 3:23) "You want justice done. Do you want it done to you?"

label: Morality and justice
title: If they say
text: "I don't need God to be good." → Agreed that you can do good things. Good by whose measure? And have you done all the good you know? (James 4:17) "Religious people do terrible things." → Yes, and you can only call them terrible if there is a standard they broke. Christianity gives you the grounds to condemn its own hypocrites. (Matt 7:21–23) "The God of the Old Testament commanded terrible things." → To judge God you need a standard above Him. Where does it come from? Then open the text: the Judge of all the earth does right, and He is patient for centuries before He judges. (Gen 18:25; Gen 15:16) "Morality is just empathy." → Empathy is a feeling, and feelings differ. Some feel none. "Is cruelty wrong for the man who feels nothing?"

label: Morality and justice
title: Bring it to the gospel
text: At the cross God did not set justice aside to show mercy. He satisfied it. Christ bore the penalty, so that God is both just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus. (Rom 3:25–26; Isa 53:5–6; 1 John 1:9) "If God judged you by your own standard, how would you do? Would you like to know how a guilty person can be declared right?" Then give The Gospel. For the way of arguing behind this page, see Worldviews.

label: For any conversation
title: The exclusivity of Christ
text: Why is Jesus the only way? We did not make this claim. Jesus did. The question is never whether Christians are narrow. It is whether what He said is true. (John 14:6; Acts 4:12)

label: The exclusivity of Christ
title: What you are showing
text: Every view of God shuts some views out. The man who says all religions lead to God is telling the Muslim, the Hindu and the Christian that each is wrong about his own faith. There is no neutral, wider place to stand. So ask which claim is true. "When you say all paths lead to God, how do you know that? And doesn't that say every religion is wrong where it disagrees with you?"

label: The exclusivity of Christ
title: What Jesus and the apostles said
text: "I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father but through Me." (John 14:6) No other name. (Acts 4:12) One God, one Mediator. (1 Tim 2:5–6) Whoever has the Son has life. (John 3:36; 1 John 5:11–12) The Old Testament says the same of God. "There is no savior besides Me." (Isa 43:11; Isa 45:22)

label: The exclusivity of Christ
title: Why there can be only one
text: Because of what the problem is. We are not lost for lack of advice. We are guilty before a holy God. Guilt needs a payment, not a path. (Rom 3:23; Rom 6:23) Because of who can pay. Only one who is truly man can stand in for men, and only one who is truly God can bear it. No one else is both. (Heb 2:17; Col 2:9; Ps 49:7–8) Because of what the cross means. If there were another way, the Father would have taken it. Christ asked in the garden. (Matt 26:39; Gal 2:21) Because He rose. No other founder left an empty tomb. God gave proof to everyone by raising Him. (Acts 17:31; Rom 1:4)

label: The exclusivity of Christ
title: The religions do not agree
text: They cannot all be true, because they contradict each other on the very things that matter: who God is, who Jesus is, and how a sinner is made right. Every other religion says do. The gospel says done. (Eph 2:8–9; John 19:30)

label: The exclusivity of Christ
title: If they say
text: "That's arrogant." → It would be, if we were the way. We are beggars telling other beggars where the bread is. Arrogance is deciding for God how He must save. (1 Cor 4:7; Titus 3:5) "What about people who never heard?" → No one is condemned for not hearing. Men are condemned for sin against the light they have: creation and conscience. That is why we go. (Rom 1:18–20; Rom 2:12–16; Rom 10:13–15) "You have heard. What will you do with it?" "Sincere people in other religions will be fine." → Sincerity does not change what is true. A man can sincerely take the wrong medicine. (Prov 14:12; Rom 10:1–3) "All religions teach basically the same thing." → On ethics there is overlap. On God and salvation they are opposites. Ask him to name what Islam, Hinduism and Christianity each say about Jesus. "It's exclusive, so it's intolerant." → The way is narrow, and the invitation is as wide as the world. "Whoever will call on the name of the Lord will be saved." (Matt 7:13–14; Rom 10:13; John 6:37; Rev 22:17) "That's true for you." → Jesus did not say He was a way for some. He rose in public history, or He did not.

label: The exclusivity of Christ
title: Bring it to the gospel
text: The only way is an open way. He turns away no one who comes. (John 6:37; Matt 11:28; Isa 55:1) "If He is the only way to the Father, are you on it?" Then give The Gospel.

label: For any conversation
title: The resurrection
text: Historical evidence that Jesus rose from the dead. Christianity stands or falls here, and Paul says so. If Christ has not been raised, our faith is worthless. He has been raised, and God has given proof of it to everyone. Give the evidence as God's facts, not as an exhibit for a neutral judge. (1 Cor 15:14; 1 Cor 15:17; Acts 17:31)

label: The resurrection
title: What you are showing
text: The resurrection was preached in the city where it happened, within weeks, in front of the people who had killed Him and could have produced the body. It was not a legend that grew far away over centuries. (Acts 2:22–24; Acts 2:32; Acts 26:26) "If Jesus really rose from the dead, would you follow Him? If not, is evidence really the issue?"

label: The resurrection
title: The facts to account for
text: He died. Roman soldiers knew when a man was dead, and a spear confirmed it. (John 19:33–35; Mark 15:44–45) He was buried in a known tomb, belonging to a member of the council. (Mark 15:43–46) The tomb was empty on the third day. The authorities never denied it. They explained it by saying the body was stolen. (Matt 28:11–15) Women found it first. No one inventing the story in that world would have chosen witnesses the courts did not accept. (Luke 24:1–11; John 20:1–2) He appeared to many, over forty days. To individuals, to groups, to more than five hundred at once, most of them still alive when Paul wrote. They ate with Him and touched Him. (1 Cor 15:3–8; Luke 24:36–43; Acts 1:3) The witnesses were changed. Men who ran and hid went out and preached it, and suffered for it. People die for what they believe is true. No one dies for what he knows he made up. (Acts 4:18–20; Acts 5:40–42) Enemies believed. James, who had not believed in his brother, and Saul, who was hunting Christians, each said he saw the risen Christ. (John 7:5; 1 Cor 15:7–8; Gal 1:13–16) It was foretold. (Ps 16:10; Isa 53:10–11; Matt 16:21)

label: The resurrection
title: The summary Paul received
text: The statement in 1 Corinthians 15:3–5 is one Paul says he was handed. He met Peter and James in Jerusalem within a few years of the cross. This is testimony from the beginning, from the men who were there. (1 Cor 15:3–5; Gal 1:18–19)

label: The resurrection
title: If they say
text: "The disciples stole the body." → Then they suffered and died for what they knew was a fraud, and not one of them broke. And the guards' story is "we were asleep, and we saw who did it." (Matt 28:11–15) "He didn't really die." → A man scourged, crucified and speared does not roll a stone, overpower guards and convince anyone he is the Lord of life. (John 19:33–34) "They hallucinated." → Groups do not share one hallucination, and not over forty days in different places. And the tomb would still hold the body. (1 Cor 15:6; Luke 24:39–43) "They went to the wrong tomb." → Then the authorities only had to go to the right one. "It's a legend that grew later." → The claim is in the earliest sources, in the names of living witnesses, in the city where it happened. (1 Cor 15:3–8; Luke 1:1–4) "Dead men don't rise. Miracles are impossible." → No one says men rise by nature. The claim is that God raised Him. That is only impossible if there is no God, which is the very thing in question. (Acts 26:8; Jer 32:17) "The Gospels contradict each other." → Witnesses who agree on the event and differ in what they include are what honest testimony looks like. See Is the Bible reliable?

label: The resurrection
title: Watch out
text: Evidence does not raise the dead. Men saw Lazarus walk out and plotted to kill him. If they do not hear Moses and the Prophets, they will not be persuaded if someone rises from the dead. Pray, and preach. (John 12:9–11; Luke 16:31) Don't argue "probably." The apostles announced it. (Acts 2:36) Don't stop at the fact. Say what it means.

label: The resurrection
title: What it means
text: Jesus is who He said He is. (Rom 1:4) The payment was accepted. He was raised for our justification. (Rom 4:25) Death is beaten. Those who are His will be raised. (1 Cor 15:20–22; John 11:25–26) A day of judgment is fixed, and the Judge has been named. (Acts 17:30–31) "He is alive today. What will you do with a living Lord?" Then give The Gospel. For the short version to run live, open the resurrection play.

label: For any conversation
title: Hell and eternal judgment
text: Why would a loving God send people to hell? Speak about hell the way Jesus did: plainly, often, and with tears. He said more about it than anyone in Scripture, and He is the one who went to the cross to save people from it. (Matt 10:28; Luke 19:41; Matt 23:37)

label: Hell and eternal judgment
title: What you are showing
text: The question assumes we are basically good people and God is overreacting. Scripture says the opposite about both. Once a man sees who God is and what sin is, the question changes from "How could God send anyone to hell?" to "How could God let anyone into heaven?" (Rom 3:10–12; Rom 3:23; Hab 1:13) "Do you think anything deserves judgment? Then who decides what, and how much?"

label: Hell and eternal judgment
title: What Scripture says
text: Hell is real, conscious and eternal. Jesus uses the same word for the punishment and for the life. (Matt 25:41; Matt 25:46; Rev 14:11; Rev 20:10) It is judgment, not an accident. It is the just sentence of a holy Judge on real guilt. (Rev 20:11–15; Rom 2:5–6; 2 Thess 1:8–9) It is fair. God judges each one according to his deeds and according to the light he had. (Rom 2:6; Luke 12:47–48; Gen 18:25) No one is there who wanted Christ. Men love darkness and will not come to the light. (John 3:19–20; John 5:40) God takes no pleasure in it. (Ezek 33:11; 2 Pet 3:9) There is no second chance after death. (Heb 9:27; Luke 16:26)

label: Hell and eternal judgment
title: Why it is eternal
text: Because of who is sinned against. The weight of a wrong rises with the worth of the one wronged. Sin is against an infinitely holy God. (Ps 51:4; Isa 6:3–5) Because sinners there do not stop sinning. Hell does not make anyone repent. (Rev 16:9–11) Because the cross shows what sin costs. If sin were small, the Son of God would not have had to die for it. (Rom 8:32; Isa 53:10)

label: Hell and eternal judgment
title: If they say
text: "A loving God wouldn't do that." → A God who shrugged at rape and murder would not be loving. Love for victims requires justice. And His love is not a guess: He gave His Son. (Rom 5:8; John 3:16; Nah 1:3) "Eternal punishment for a few years of sin isn't fair." → Time spent sinning is not how we measure a crime. A murder takes a moment. And see "Why it is eternal" above. "I'm a good person." → By whose standard? Walk through the commandments. See The Way of the Master. (James 2:10; Rom 3:19–20) "God sends people to hell for not believing in Jesus." → People are condemned for their sin. Jesus is the rescue they refuse. A man does not die because he refused the doctor, but from the disease. (John 3:17–18; John 3:36) "What about those who never heard?" → See The exclusivity of Christ. (Rom 1:18–20) "Hell is just separation from God" / "the wicked are simply destroyed." → Jesus describes fire, darkness, weeping and a punishment as lasting as eternal life. (Matt 13:41–42; Matt 25:46; Mark 9:47–48) "I'd rather be in hell with my friends." → There is no friendship there. Every good thing you have ever enjoyed came from the God you would be without. (James 1:17; Luke 16:23–28)

label: Hell and eternal judgment
title: Watch out
text: Don't soften what Jesus said, and don't enjoy saying it. Paul warned people with tears. (Acts 20:31; Rom 9:1–3) Don't pronounce on a particular dead person. Say God will do right, and turn to the living man in front of you. (Gen 18:25) Don't use hell as a threat to win. It is a warning from someone who was headed there too. (Eph 2:3–5; 2 Cor 5:11) Don't leave him there. Hell is never the end of the conversation.

label: Hell and eternal judgment
title: Bring it to the gospel
text: On the cross Christ bore the wrath of God for sinners. Everyone's sin will be punished: either in hell, or in Him. That is why no one has to go. (Isa 53:5–6; Gal 3:13; 1 Thess 1:10; Rom 8:1) "He took what sinners deserve so they could go free. Will you turn from your sin and trust Him?" Then give The Gospel.

label: For any conversation
title: Faith and reason
text: Is believing in God irrational, or blind faith? Biblical faith is not belief without evidence, and it is not a leap in the dark. It is trust in a Person who has spoken and has proved Himself trustworthy. And reason is not faith's rival. It is a gift from the God the unbeliever is using it against. (Heb 11:1; Isa 1:18; Prov 1:7)

label: Faith and reason
title: What you are showing
text: Everyone trusts something he cannot prove first: his senses, his memory, his reason, the order of nature. The unbeliever has faith too. The question is not faith or reason. It is which faith makes reason possible. See Worldviews. "What do you trust that you can't prove? Why do you trust your own mind?"

label: Faith and reason
title: What faith is
text: Faith is trust in what God has said. Abraham was fully assured that what God had promised, He was able to do. (Rom 4:20–21; Heb 11:1; Heb 11:6) It rests on what God has done in public. The apostles appealed to what was seen, heard and touched, and said it was not done in a corner. (1 John 1:1–3; Luke 1:1–4; Acts 26:25–26; 2 Pet 1:16) It comes by hearing the word of Christ. (Rom 10:17; John 20:30–31) It is a gift. No one reasons himself into the kingdom. God opens blind eyes. (Eph 2:8–9; 2 Cor 4:4–6; 1 Cor 2:14)

label: Faith and reason
title: What reason is
text: God commands us to think. "Come now, and let us reason together." We are to love Him with all our mind. (Isa 1:18; Matt 22:37; Rom 12:2) The apostles reasoned. Paul reasoned from the Scriptures, explaining and giving evidence. We are told to be ready with a defense. (Acts 17:2–3; Acts 18:4; 1 Pet 3:15) Reason has a starting point. The fear of the Lord is the beginning of knowledge. All the treasures of wisdom are hidden in Christ. (Prov 1:7; Col 2:3; Ps 36:9) Reason is a tool, not the judge. It is used under God's word, and it is bent by sin like the rest of us. (Rom 1:21–22; 2 Cor 10:5; Eph 4:17–18)

label: Faith and reason
title: If they say
text: "Faith is believing without evidence." → That is not how the Bible uses the word. You have faith in your wife or your surgeon because of what you know of them. "Do you trust anyone you've never tested in a lab?" "I only believe what can be proven by science." → That sentence cannot be proven by science. And science itself runs on trust that nature is orderly and our minds can know it. (Gen 8:22; Col 1:17) "Science has replaced God." → Science explains how things in the world work. It does not explain why there is a world, why it is orderly, or why we can understand it. Modern science grew among men who expected order because they believed in a Lawgiver. "Smart people don't believe." → Many do, and always have. But truth is not settled by counting, and God chose what the world calls foolish to shame the wise. (1 Cor 1:20–27) "You believe because you were raised that way." → Where a belief came from does not tell you whether it is true. He was raised to believe things too. "Show me God and I'll believe." → He has shown Himself in what He made, in conscience, in Scripture, and in His Son. People saw Jesus raise the dead and still refused. (Rom 1:19–20; John 12:37; John 14:9) "If I can't understand it, I won't accept it." → He accepts many things he cannot fully understand. And a God we could fit inside our heads would not be God. (Isa 55:8–9; Rom 11:33)

label: Faith and reason
title: Watch out
text: Don't apologize for starting with Scripture. Everyone starts somewhere. Don't set faith against thinking. Don't say "you just have to believe." Give a reason. (1 Pet 3:15) Don't think a good argument saves. The problem is not the mind alone, but the heart that suppresses the truth. (Rom 1:18; John 3:19)

label: Faith and reason
title: Bring it to the gospel
text: The most reasonable thing a creature can do is believe his Creator. God has spoken, He has come, and He has raised His Son in proof. (Heb 1:1–2; Acts 17:31) "If God has spoken, is it more reasonable to trust Him or to trust yourself?" Then give The Gospel.

label: For any conversation
title: The fallacy of evolution
text: Why evolution cannot stand, and why creation is true. God made the heavens, the earth and everything in them in six days, and He made man directly, in His image (Gen 1:1; Gen 1:27; Gen 2:7; Ex 20:11). That is our starting point, not our conclusion. Evolution is not a discovery that forced itself on honest observers. It is the origin story of a worldview that has already ruled God out. (Rom 1:20–22; 2 Pet 3:3–6)

label: The fallacy of evolution
title: What you are showing
text: You and he look at the same fossils, the same rocks and the same DNA. The difference is not the evidence. It is the starting point each of you reads it with. No one watched the beginning, and no one can repeat it in a lab. One Witness was there, and He has told us what He did. (Job 38:4; Heb 11:3; Ps 33:6; Ps 33:9) "Were you there? Then whose account of the beginning are you trusting, and why?"

label: The fallacy of evolution
title: The starting point decides the answer
text: Many of evolution's own defenders say so. Harvard geneticist Richard Lewontin wrote that scientists accept material explanations because of a prior commitment to materialism, and that "we cannot allow a Divine Foot in the door" (New York Review of Books, January 9, 1997). That is a rule about what answers are allowed, made before the evidence is looked at. "If God did create, would your method ever be allowed to find that out?"

label: The fallacy of evolution
title: What evolution cannot give you
text: Ask one question at a time and wait for the answer. A beginning. Something does not come from nothing. "Where did matter, energy and the laws they follow come from?" (Gen 1:1; John 1:3) Life. Life has only ever been seen to come from life. Natural selection can only work on something already alive and reproducing, so it cannot explain the first living thing. "How did the first life arise, and has anyone ever seen it happen?" Information. DNA is a code: instructions, stored and read. Everywhere else we find a code, we know a mind wrote it. "Have you ever seen a message write itself?" (Ps 139:13–16) Kinds. We see change within kinds: dog breeds, finch beaks, bacteria that resist a drug. They are still dogs, finches and bacteria. That is variation in what God made "after their kind." It is not one kind turning into another. "Is that change you've watched, or change you've been told happened?" (Gen 1:21; Gen 1:24–25) A mind you can trust. If your brain is the product of survival and not of truth, you have no reason to trust its conclusions, including evolution. Darwin felt this. He wrote of his "horrid doubt" whether the convictions of a mind developed from lower animals "are of any value or at all trustworthy" (letter to William Graham, July 3, 1881). "Why trust a brain that was shaped only to survive?" See Worldviews. Right and wrong. If we are animals shaped by survival of the fittest, there is no "ought." The strong removing the weak is simply how the process works. He does not live that way, because he is made in God's image. "If evolution is true, what makes cruelty wrong?" (Gen 9:6; Rom 2:14–15) Worth and purpose. An accident has no purpose and no worth beyond what it can do. Every person you meet knows better. (Ps 100:3; Eccl 3:11; Col 1:16)

label: The fallacy of evolution
title: Not enough time (Haldane's dilemma)
text: This argument comes from evolution's own side. Eric Hovind (Creation Today) and John Harris (Living Waters Europe) take it to college campuses, and Walter ReMine set it out in The Biotic Message (1993). The man. J. B. S. Haldane was one of the founders of population genetics and a committed evolutionist. In 1957 he published "The Cost of Natural Selection." The cost. For a helpful mutation to spread to a whole population, those without it have to die out, generation after generation. A population can only afford so many of those deaths at once. Haldane's estimate: about one beneficial change fixed every 300 generations. The time. Give evolution 10 million years from an ape-like ancestor to man, which is more than evolutionists ask for. At 20 years a generation that is 500,000 generations. The total. 500,000 ÷ 300 is about 1,667 beneficial changes. That is all natural selection can afford. The gap. Human and chimp DNA were long said to be 1% different. In a genome of 3 billion letters that is 30 million differences. A 2025 comparison of complete ape genomes found that around 15% of the two genomes does not line up one-to-one (Nature, Yoo et al.). Either way the gap is millions of letters, and selection can pay for fewer than two thousand. Even with every allowance. Suppose one beneficial change were fixed every single generation, 300 times faster than Haldane found. You would still have only 500,000. "Can 1,667 changes turn an ape-like creature into a man who speaks, writes, builds and worships?" What he will say back: "That was solved. Kimura showed most changes are neutral." → Look at what that answer gives up. In 1968 Motoo Kimura agreed that selection could not account for that many changes, so he proposed that most of them are neutral and spread by chance (drift). Neutral means it helps nothing. "Then what built the human brain, speech and upright walking: selection, which is too slow, or chance, which selects nothing?" "Not every difference has to be beneficial, and the differences are split between two lines." → Fine. Take away as many as he likes. The question is whether fewer than two thousand useful changes can make a man. "Haldane's math is from 1957." → Haldane expected it to be revised, and evolutionists have been revising it ever since. "What is the number today, and does it get you from thousands to millions?" "One study can't overturn hundreds." → Truth is not counted by hands. One sound measurement can overturn a consensus, and it has before. "If the numbers are right, would it matter how many people believed otherwise?" "I'm not a biologist. I can't answer that." → Thank him for the honest answer and don't press. "Would you look into it? And if evolution can't do it, are you willing to ask who made you?"

label: The fallacy of evolution
title: Why creation is true
text: God says so, and He was there. Scripture is the standard, not the thing on trial. (Gen 1:31; Ex 20:11; Ps 33:6; Ps 33:9; Neh 9:6) Jesus says so. He treated Genesis as history: God made them male and female "from the beginning of creation," not after ages of animal ancestry. (Mark 10:6; Matt 19:4–5; Luke 11:50–51) Creation says so. What God made shows His power and nature so clearly that everyone is without excuse. (Rom 1:20; Ps 19:1–4; Isa 45:18) The gospel depends on it. Adam was a real man (Luke 3:38). Through that one man sin entered the world, and death through sin (Rom 5:12). Christ is the last Adam, who undoes what the first Adam did (1 Cor 15:21–22; 1 Cor 15:45). If death was here for ages before Adam, death is not the wages of sin, and the cross answers a problem that was never real.

label: The fallacy of evolution
title: Can't God have used evolution?
text: Some Christians say so to keep the peace. It costs too much. It puts death, disease and suffering before sin, in a world God called "very good." (Gen 1:31; Rom 5:12; Rom 8:20–22) It turns Adam into a symbol, when Luke, Paul and Jesus treat him as a man. (Luke 3:38; Rom 5:14; 1 Cor 15:45) It makes the days mean something the fourth commandment does not allow: Israel worked six days and rested one because God did. (Ex 20:9–11) It lets the changing opinions of men correct the word of God. (Isa 40:8; Mark 7:13) It calls good what God calls an enemy. If death built us, death is the tool of creation. Scripture says death is "the last enemy" that Christ will abolish. (1 Cor 15:26; Rev 21:4) It gives you a different God. An evolutionist saw this plainly. Philosopher David Hull wrote that the God implied by evolution is "careless, wasteful, indifferent, almost diabolical," not the sort of God anyone would pray to (Nature, August 8, 1991). The God of the Bible made a world without death, and sin ruined it. (Gen 1:31; Rom 8:20–22)

label: The fallacy of evolution
title: If he says
text: "Evolution is a proven fact. All scientists agree." → A count of hands is not a proof, and the majority has been wrong before. "Which part has been observed: change within a kind, or one kind becoming another?" "Small changes add up. Give it millions of years." → That is the claim, not the evidence. What we observe is variation inside a kind, using information already there. "Has anyone watched the small changes add up to a new kind, or is that the part you take on trust?" And see the time problem above. "The fossils show it." → Fossils show that things died and were buried, most of them suddenly, in water-laid rock, all over the earth. That fits a worldwide flood. A fossil does not come with a date or a list of its children. And soft tissue, including flexible vessels and what look like cells, has been recovered from dinosaur bone (Mary Schweitzer, Science, 2005). "How does that last 65 million years?" (Gen 7:19–23; 2 Pet 3:5–6) "We share 98% of our DNA with chimps." → Similar design points to one Designer as easily as to one ancestor. A builder uses the same materials in different houses. And the differences that remain are the difference between an ape and a man who writes symphonies and prays. (Gen 1:26–27) "Radiometric dating proves billions of years." → The measurement is of what is in the rock today. The age is a calculation that assumes how much was there at the start, that nothing was added or lost, and that the rate never changed. No one was there to check any of the three. Creation researchers also report carbon-14 in coal and diamonds said to be millions of years old, where none should be left after about 100,000 years (the RATE project, 2005). "How do you know the starting amount?" "That's religion, not science." → Both are claims about a past no one can repeat. And modern science grew up among men who expected order because they believed in a Lawgiver: Kepler, Boyle, Newton, Faraday, Maxwell. "Why should a universe that came from nothing obey laws at all?" "You're using God to fill the gaps." → No. We reason from what we do know: codes come from minds, and life comes from life. He is the one filling the gaps, with time and chance. "Is 'given enough time, it happened' an observation or a hope?" "With infinite time, or infinite universes, anything can happen." → No one has observed another universe, so that is faith, not science. And time cannot be infinite into the past. Picture an endless row of falling dominoes: if an infinite number had to fall before yours, yours would never fall. We have reached today, so there was a first day. (Gen 1:1) "Then who made God?" → Whatever begins needs a cause. God has no beginning. He is not one more thing inside the universe that needs explaining. He is the reason there is anything to explain. (Ps 90:2; Isa 40:28) "Genesis is poetry." → Genesis 1 is written as Hebrew narrative, with numbered days, evening and morning. Moses, Jesus and Paul all read it as history. (Ex 20:11; Mark 10:6; Rom 5:12–14)

label: The fallacy of evolution
title: Watch out
text: Don't say "there's no evidence for evolution." He will show you evidence of change within kinds and think he has won. Say: same evidence, different starting point. Don't say "it's only a theory," "why are there still monkeys?" or "the second law of thermodynamics disproves it." Creation ministries themselves tell Christians to drop these. They are easy to answer and cost you the hearing. Don't repeat stories you can't source, such as Darwin recanting on his deathbed. He did not. Use Haldane's argument in its strong form. Say "about 1,667 beneficial changes," not "30 million changes times 20 years is 600 million years." The short version treats every difference as a beneficial change in one line of descent, and anyone who has read about it will answer that most differences are neutral and are shared between two lines. Then you are defending your arithmetic and not making your point. Don't say "no one has ever answered it." They have answered, by giving up natural selection as the main cause. Say that. Say where the 15% comes from. It is the share of the two genomes that does not line up one-to-one in the 2025 comparison. He may say it is counted differently; the 1% figure makes the argument just as well. Don't make it a contest. No bets, no crowd, no gloating when he has no answer. You want him, not the win. (Col 4:5–6) Don't make it the main thing. A man can give up evolution and still be lost. The aim is the Creator he answers to, and the Savior he needs. (Acts 17:24–31) Stay kind. Many have never heard evolution questioned. Ask, don't mock. (2 Tim 2:24–26; 1 Pet 3:15)

label: The fallacy of evolution
title: Bring it to the gospel
text: The One who made him is the One he has sinned against. The Creator entered His own creation, died for sinners and rose again, and He now commands all people everywhere to repent. (John 1:3; John 1:14; Col 1:16; Col 1:19–20; Acts 17:30–31) "If you were made, you belong to Someone. Are you ready to meet Him?" Then give The Gospel. For the short answer to use live, open the evolution answer.

label: For any conversation
title: The abolition of abortion
text: You shall not murder. The child in the womb is a human being made in the image of God, and worth exactly what you are worth. That is why abortion is not to be regulated or reduced but ended: the protection every born person has belongs to the unborn too. This page is about the value of that child. It rests on Scripture, and it is brought to people with the gospel. (Ex 20:13; Gen 1:27; Gen 9:6; Prov 24:11–12)

label: The abolition of abortion
title: What you are showing
text: The whole question turns on one thing: what is the unborn? If it is not a human being, no justification for abortion is needed. If it is a human being, no justification is enough. Scripture and plain observation give the same answer: from conception this is a living human being, a neighbor, and God's image bearer. (Gen 1:27; Ps 139:13–16) "What is it? If it is a human being, what would justify killing it?"

label: The abolition of abortion
title: A human being from conception
text: This is biology, not opinion. When a sperm fertilizes an egg, a new, living, distinct human being exists, with his own DNA. The embryology textbooks used in universities, such as Langman's Medical Embryology, begin human development at fertilization. these are stages, not kinds. Each names how far along a human being is, the way "toddler" and "teenager" do. Nothing becomes human by growing. He is human, and he grows. "Fetus" is Latin for offspring. Only four things differ between him and you. Pastor Jeff Durbin puts it this way: size, level of development, environment and degree of dependence. "When do we kill people because of their size?" A seven-year-old is not fully developed. A newborn is wholly dependent. Each of us will be dependent again if we live long enough. You were once exactly that. Every person you will ever meet was once a human embryo. "You are here because your mother did not choose otherwise. Why wouldn't we do for them what we would want done for us?" (Matt 7:12)

label: The abolition of abortion
title: What God says about the unborn
text: God forms each one. He knits the child together in the womb and writes its days before one of them exists. (Ps 139:13–16; Job 31:15; Isa 44:24) God knows them as persons. He knew Jeremiah before he was born. John leaped in the womb at the presence of the unborn Christ. Scripture uses the same word for the baby in the womb and the baby in the manger. (Jer 1:5; Luke 1:41–44; Luke 2:12) God became one. The Son of God took on flesh at conception, not at birth. (Luke 1:31; Luke 1:35) Children are a gift, not a burden to be removed. (Ps 127:3) He is the fatherless child God tells us to defend. A fatherless child is one with no one to speak for him and no one to protect him. Durbin: there is "no more fatherless child in this world" than the one abandoned in the womb. God told His own people that He would not hear their prayers while their hands were full of blood, and then said: seek justice, correct oppression, bring justice to the fatherless. The promise that scarlet sins will be white as snow comes in the very next breath. (Isa 1:15–18) He is your neighbor. Love your neighbor as yourself. (Mark 12:31; Luke 10:36–37)

label: The abolition of abortion
title: What God says about shedding innocent blood
text: "You shall not murder." (Ex 20:13) The image of God is why murder is a capital matter. (Gen 9:6) God hates hands that shed innocent blood. (Prov 6:16–17) Sacrificing children brings guilt on a whole land. Israel offered its sons and daughters, and the land was polluted with blood. (Ps 106:37–38; Lev 18:21; Jer 7:31) The law of Moses protected the child in the womb. Harm to the child was answered life for life. (Ex 21:22–25)

label: The abolition of abortion
title: Why abolition, and not regulation
text: God does not ask a nation to sin less. He says to stop, and to do justice. (Isa 1:16–17; Amos 5:15; Amos 5:24) You would accept it nowhere else. No one would praise a law that allowed slavery so long as the quarters were clean, or trafficking so long as the victims were over sixteen. A law that says a child may be killed before so many weeks, or must be buried properly afterward, is the same kind of law. Durbin: "You don't change it through compromise, you change it through the truth." We may not do evil that good may come. (Rom 3:8) A law that says "and then you may kill the child" is an unjust law. A rule that allows it before a heartbeat, before so many weeks, or after a waiting period still says that some children may be killed. Woe to those who decree unjust statutes. (Isa 10:1–2; Ex 23:7; Prov 17:15) Justice does not show partiality. The unborn child is owed the same protection of the law as any born person, with no difference for age, size, place or how he was conceived. (Lev 19:15; Deut 1:17; James 2:9) This is what the ruler is for. God gave the governing authority the sword to punish the one who does evil. Protecting the innocent from being killed is the first duty of any government. (Rom 13:3–4; Prov 31:8–9; Ps 82:3–4) This is how slavery was fought. The men who ended the slave trade did not ask for kinder slavery. They called it sin and demanded its end. Biblical, not secular. We do not leave the Bible out to sound reasonable. Abortion is sin, and the answer to sin is repentance and the gospel. (Isa 10:1; Dan 11:32)

label: The abolition of abortion
title: The same protection
text: Everything the law does for a child after birth, it should do for him before birth, and for the same reason: he is one of us. We do not ask for a special law for the unborn. We ask that they no longer be left out of the law that already protects everyone else. (Lev 19:15; Prov 31:8–9; Ps 82:3–4)

label: The abolition of abortion
title: If the child would suffer
text: This is the argument you will hear most: he will be poor, sick, unwanted, born to addicts, or live only minutes. It says that because a child may suffer, it is kinder to kill him first. It does not hold. We never reason this way about anyone else. We do not kill the homeless man, the addict or the veteran on the street because their lives are hard. We help them. "You know what you can't do to someone who is suffering? Kill them." Move the child one day past birth. A mother learns on the day her son is born that his father is going to prison and his life will be hard. May she kill him to spare him? If not, what changed except which side of the womb he is on? No one can see a child's future. Durbin's son Augustine was diagnosed in the womb with severe spina bifida, and his birth mother said no one would want him now. A Christian friend stood between her and the abortion clinic and found a family. He was born whole. Dying is not the same as being killed. A child who will live ten minutes can be held, named and loved for ten minutes. A miscarriage or a stillbirth is a grief. Abortion is a decision. "Easing suffering is something we should do. Killing the one who suffers is not how we do it." The answer to a hard life is help. That is where the church comes in: with a home, with money, with adoption. (James 1:27; Ps 68:5–6; Gal 6:2) Suffering is not the last word. God gives life, numbers its days and can redeem any of them. (Ps 139:16; John 9:1–3; Rom 8:18) "If suffering ahead is a reason to kill someone, who among us is safe?"

label: The abolition of abortion
title: If they say
text: "My body, my choice." → There are two bodies. The child has his own DNA, his own heartbeat, and often a different blood type and sex. "Whose body is being ended?" "It's just a clump of cells." → So are you, a larger one. Size, development, location and dependence are the only differences between the unborn and the born. "Which of those four makes it right to kill a person?" "It's not a person until it's viable, or born." → Viability measures our hospitals, not his humanity; it moves every decade. A newborn cannot survive on his own either. "What changed in the eight inches of the birth canal?" "What about rape?" → Rape is a terrible crime, and the rapist should be punished severely. The child did not commit it. Scripture says the child is not put to death for the father's sin. Killing the child does not undo the crime; it adds a second victim. (Deut 24:16; Ezek 18:20) "What about the life of the mother?" → Then there are two patients, and a doctor fights for both. Treating a mother to save her life, when her child dies in spite of every effort to save him, is not abortion. Deliberately killing the child is. Removing an ectopic pregnancy and caring for a miscarriage are not abortion either. "It can't survive without me. It isn't autonomous." → Neither can a newborn, or a man on a ventilator. Needing someone has never made a person less of one. It makes us more responsible for him. "Is a child worth less the more he needs you?" "It isn't conscious. It can't think or feel." → A sleeping man is not conscious, and a man under anesthesia feels nothing. We may not kill either. "Alive and human" is biology. "Conscious enough to count" is a philosophy someone made up, and it could exclude a newborn as easily. "How conscious does a human being have to be before he has the right to live?" "Legally, you're a person when you're born." → The law once said a slave was property and a Jew was not a citizen. "If the law changed tomorrow to say three-year-olds aren't persons, would that make it right?" Law does not decide what a human being is worth. God already has. "You're a man. You don't get a say." → Whether a child is a human being does not depend on who is asking. "I'm not telling you what to do with your body. I'm speaking for the body inside your body." "Have you adopted any? Then you can't talk." → A man can oppose child trafficking without adopting every victim. And Christians do adopt, foster and give more than anyone. "If I adopt this child today, may he live?" "Women will die without it." → Death in childbirth in this country is rare, and every doctor may treat a mother whose life is in danger (see the answer above on the life of the mother). Hard cases are a reason to care for two patients well. They are not a reason for a million elective abortions a year. "It's a religious issue. Christians used the Bible to defend slavery." → Some twisted it that way. The Christians who ended the slave trade answered them from Scripture: man is made in God's image, and man-stealing was a capital crime in the law of Moses. The church has spoken the same way about abortion from the start. The Didache, written within a lifetime of the apostles, says, "You shall not murder a child by abortion." (Ex 21:16; Gen 1:27) "The baby will be poor, disabled or unwanted." → We do not kill born people for being poor, disabled or unwanted. His worth is the image of God, not his prospects. See "If the child would suffer" above. "You can't legislate morality." → Every law does. Laws against theft, rape and murder all enforce a moral judgment. The only question is whose. (Rom 13:3–4) "You only care until the baby is born." → Even if that were true of someone, it would not make killing right. And it is not true: Christians run most of the pregnancy centers, adoptions and foster homes in this country. "If I adopt the child, may he live?" "That's your religion." → That a new human life begins at conception is biology. That it is wrong to kill an innocent human being is a moral claim everyone makes for the born. "On what basis do you leave out the unborn?" See Worldviews.

label: The abolition of abortion
title: It is a matter of the heart
text: Biology is on our side, and it is not enough. Most people already know what is in the womb; that is why they call it a "choice." Durbin: "The issue is sin." A child is seen as a burden because we put ourselves first, and only a new heart stops wanting that. So give the facts, and then give the gospel, which is the power of God for salvation. (Rom 1:16; Prov 8:36; Ezek 36:26)

label: The abolition of abortion
title: To the man or woman who has done it
text: Many of the people you talk with have paid for an abortion, pressured someone into one, or had one. Do not soften what it was, and do not withhold the only remedy. It is sin, and it is not the unforgivable sin. David arranged a man's death. Paul approved of Stephen's. Both were forgiven. (Ps 51:14; Acts 8:1; 1 Tim 1:15–16) Christ's blood cleanses from all sin. "Though your sins are as scarlet, they will be as white as snow." (Isa 1:18; 1 John 1:9; 1 John 1:7) "Such were some of you." (1 Cor 6:9–11) Calling it what it is makes forgiveness possible. If we tell her nothing wrong was done, we leave her alone with a grief she cannot name. If it was sin, it can be forgiven, washed and remembered no more. (Heb 8:12; Ps 103:12) "What you did was real, and so is forgiveness. Christ died for sinners like you and me. Will you turn to Him?"

label: The abolition of abortion
title: Watch out
text: No violence, no threats, no harassment. Ever. We call on rulers to do justice through the law, and we call sinners to repent. Vengeance belongs to God, and the sword belongs to the governing authority, not to us. (Rom 12:19; Rom 13:4; James 1:20) Don't make a guilty person feel beyond hope. Speak the truth as one forgiven sinner to another. (Gal 6:1; Eph 4:15) Don't argue from politics or party. Argue from Scripture and from what the child is. Oppose the position, love the brother. Many Christians support laws that limit abortion without ending it. Say plainly why you cannot: such a law still leaves some children unprotected. And keep the fellowship. Durbin says of a pastor he disagrees with on this that he is "a better pastor and a better man" than himself. (Eph 4:2–3) Keep the child in view. The argument is not about politics, parties or punishing anyone. It is about what he is and what he is worth. If the talk drifts, bring it back: "What is the unborn?" Don't stop at the law. A man can oppose abortion and be lost. Get to the cross. (Acts 17:30–31)

label: The abolition of abortion
title: What a man can do
text: Pray. Speak up for those who cannot (Prov 31:8–9). Tell your representatives you want abortion abolished, not managed. Go with your church to the abortion clinic to plead with mothers and fathers and to offer real help. You may have fifteen seconds before the door closes. Durbin's church says something like this: "Mom, please don't do this to your baby. We're here because we love you. We will help you with anything you need. We will even adopt your baby." On their first morning out, two mothers turned around. Help a mother in need. Adopt, foster, give. And preach the gospel, because only new hearts stop wanting this. (Prov 24:11–12; Mic 6:8; James 1:27)

label: The abolition of abortion
title: Who to learn from
text: Pastor Jeff Durbin and End Abortion Now. Durbin pastors Apologia Church here in Arizona. End Abortion Now is its ministry, "dedicated to saving lives and preaching the Gospel." It trains local churches, free of charge, to minister outside abortion clinics, and it helps Christians press their lawmakers for bills of equal protection. Its aim: "We desire equal protection for all." Its goal for itself: "When abortion ends, we end." Three of Durbin's own children are adopted, and each was nearly aborted. He says, "Every single one of these babies is as valuable in the eyes of God" as his own. (endabortionnow.com) T. Russell Hunter. A historian of the nineteenth century and founder of Abolitionists Rising. He came to this work by studying the Christians who abolished slavery and asking who is treated as less than human today. Abolitionists Rising. Their stated goals are "the abolition of abortion, the repentance of the nation, and the glorification of God." Their marks: immediate and not gradual, equal protection, no exceptions, biblical and not secular, and obeying God over unjust rulings. (abolitionistsrising.com) Then give The Gospel.

label: For any conversation
title: MacArthur on Rome
text: What John MacArthur says about Roman Catholicism, in his own words. These lines come from John MacArthur's sermons on the Pope and the papacy, the Mass, the priesthood, Galatians 5 and the idolatry of Mary worship (Grace to You). Use them to know where our teachers stand and why. With a Catholic friend, open the Bible first and ask questions; these are for your own conviction and for when someone asks, "Is it really that serious?"

label: MacArthur on Rome
title: His heart
text: He begins with grief, not anger: "We find no delight in people who are condemned to hell." And he ends with a plea: "People need to be rescued from this system." (Ezek 33:11; Rom 10:1; 2 Tim 2:24–26)

label: MacArthur on Rome
title: The system
text: MacArthur calls Roman Catholicism "an apostate, corrupt, heretical, false Christianity" and "a front for the kingdom of Satan." On adding works to faith he says, "There is no room for any alteration of the gospel." Of Rome and Eastern Orthodoxy together: "It is not to be joined, it is to be cursed." He is using Paul's word, anathema. (Gal 1:6–9; Gal 5:2–4; 2 Cor 11:13–15; 2 Pet 2:1) Trent placed its curse on justification by faith alone [Sess. 6, can. 9, 12, 14] and has never withdrawn it. Paul put his curse on any gospel that adds to faith.

label: MacArthur on Rome
title: The Mass
text: He calls transubstantiation "mystical hocus-pocus, mumbo-jumbo for sure," and says that phrase came from the Latin words of the Mass, hoc est corpus meum. He says the Mass is paid for: "You pay for a Mass. That's how the coffers of the Catholic Church are filled." And he reminds us that English believers were burned alive for denying it. (Heb 9:25–28; Heb 10:10–14; Heb 10:18) Rome's own law lets a priest accept an offering to apply a Mass for a named intention [Code of Canon Law, can. 945]. Trent calls the Mass propitiatory for the living and the dead [Sess. 22, can. 3]. Archbishop John Tillotson gave the same origin for "hocus-pocus" in 1694. Rest the argument on Hebrews, and use the phrase as MacArthur's. Foxe's Book of Martyrs records about 280 people burned under Mary Tudor (1555–1558), many of them for rejecting the Mass.

label: MacArthur on Rome
title: Mary
text: "Pagan goddess worship dressed up in Roman Catholic fantasy." He traces it to the old mother-and-child cults (Ishtar, Astarte, Isis) and to the "queen of heaven" whom God judged Judah for worshiping. On "Mother of God" he says, "God was never born." On the claim that we reach Christ through Mary: "This is a Satanic fabrication." On Co-Redemptrix: not formal dogma, but "unofficial reality." (Jer 7:18; Jer 44:17–19; Luke 1:46–48; Luke 11:27–28; 1 Tim 2:5; Isa 42:8) He quotes Rome's own writers, above all Alphonsus de Liguori's The Glories of Mary, which Rome has never condemned. Liguori is a canonized saint and a Doctor of the Church. The Catechism still calls Mary Advocate, Helper, Benefactress and Mediatrix and says she was exalted "as Queen over all things" [CCC 966, 968–969]. The 2025 Vatican note set aside a title. It removed no doctrine.

label: MacArthur on Rome
title: Purgatory and indulgences
text: "Purgatory is what makes the whole system work." He says Rome invented it, that it is a second chance after death, and that indulgences are forgiveness for sale: the treasury of merit can be drawn on, and "you can buy it." (Heb 1:3; Heb 9:27; Luke 23:43; Acts 8:20) Rome still teaches the treasury of merit and indulgences for the living and the dead [CCC 1471–1479], and still grants them for acts such as passing through a Holy Door in a Jubilee year (2000, 2025). The open sale of indulgences is what Luther attacked in 1517.

label: MacArthur on Rome
title: The Pope
text: He says the titles are stolen. "Holy Father" is what Jesus called God. Head of the church belongs to Christ. And Vicar of Christ, the one who stands in Christ's place: "He has stolen that from the Holy Spirit." He says there is no evidence in Scripture that Peter was ever in Rome. He reads out the papacy's record of immorality and wealth and calls its display "theater." On Antichrist he quotes Luther, Calvin, Knox, the Puritans and Spurgeon, then gives his own view: the Pope is not the final Antichrist, but "the very embodiment of antichrist" in this age, and it is "not a bad guess to see the final Antichrist as a pope." (John 17:11; Matt 23:9; Col 1:18; John 16:7; 1 John 2:18; 2 Thess 2:3–4) This was the common Protestant confession. Luther's Smalcald Articles (II.4), the Westminster Confession (25.6) and the 1689 London Baptist Confession (26.4) all name the Pope as "that Antichrist, that man of sin." Our church teaches a future, personal Antichrist. MacArthur's wording fits that: many antichrists now (1 John 2:18), the final one still to come.

label: MacArthur on Rome
title: The priesthood
text: On required celibacy he goes to 1 Timothy 4: "Those who forbid marriage are advocating a doctrine of demons." He ties the scandals of the priesthood to that rule and to a priesthood the New Testament never created. (1 Tim 4:1–3; 1 Tim 3:2; 1 Cor 9:5; 1 Pet 2:9)

label: MacArthur on Rome
title: How it began
text: "What was born with Constantine was Christendom rather than Christianity." He says the empire made one official religion, pagan practice came in with the crowds, and true believers were there through every century, protesting. Constantine legalized Christianity in 313 and called the Council of Nicaea in 325. Theodosius made it the state religion in 380. The papal claims grew after that: Leo I (440–461), then Gregory VII and Boniface VIII in the Middle Ages.

label: MacArthur on Rome
title: Why people stay
text: From John 5, where a man healed by Jesus sides with the leaders against Him: "That is the power of false religion." People fear being put out. Expect it, and pray. (John 5:15–16; John 9:22; 2 Cor 10:4–5; 2 Cor 4:4) Then go to the Catholic plays and give The Gospel.

label: The Trinity
title: There is one God
text: (Deut 6:4; Isa 43:10; Isa 44:6; 1 Cor 8:4; James 2:19)

label: The Trinity
title: The Son is God
text: (John 1:1; John 8:58; John 20:28; Col 2:9; Titus 2:13; Heb 1:8) For why only God can redeem, open Only God can pay the ransom.

label: The Trinity
title: The Holy Spirit is God
text: (Acts 5:3–4; 1 Cor 3:16; Ps 139:7–8; Heb 3:7–11) For the full argument, open The Holy Spirit play.

label: The Trinity
title: The three are distinct Persons
text: The Father sends the Son, the Son prays to the Father, and the Spirit is sent by both. All three are present at Jesus' baptism. (Matt 3:16–17; Matt 28:19; John 14:16–17; John 15:26; John 17:5; Gal 4:4–6; 2 Cor 13:14)

label: The Trinity
title: What it is not
text: that is tritheism. Scripture says there is one God. that is modalism. The Father, Son and Spirit speak to and about one another. that is Arianism. All things were made through the Son (John 1:3). "Which of these lines do you disagree with? Let's read the verses for that one."

title: Is the Bible reliable?
text: Muslims, Mormons and atheists all attack this from different sides.

label: Is the Bible reliable?
title: We have what they wrote
text: The New Testament survives in thousands of Greek manuscripts, some copied within a few generations of the originals. The Dead Sea Scrolls, copied before and around the time of Christ, agree closely with the Hebrew manuscripts copied a thousand years later. (Isa 40:8; Matt 24:35; 1 Pet 1:24–25)

label: Is the Bible reliable?
title: It comes from eyewitnesses
text: The writers were eyewitnesses or wrote down what eyewitnesses told them, while many witnesses were still alive to object. (Luke 1:1–4; 2 Pet 1:16; 1 John 1:1–3; 1 Cor 15:3–8)

label: Is the Bible reliable?
title: Jesus treated Scripture as God's word
text: He quoted it as final, said it cannot be broken, and said every part of it would be fulfilled. (Matt 4:4; Matt 5:17–18; John 10:35; Luke 24:44)

label: Is the Bible reliable?
title: God breathed it out
text: Men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit, so the Scriptures as first written are without error. (2 Tim 3:16–17; 2 Pet 1:20–21)

label: Is the Bible reliable?
title: Prophecy written centuries ahead
text: The suffering Servant, the pierced hands and feet, the birthplace of the Messiah and the pierced One were all written long before Jesus was born. (Isa 53:5–6; Ps 22:16; Mic 5:2; Zech 12:10)
